design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person crossover laboratory study at the UCSF Clinical Research Center (San Francisco General Hospital), during a single three-evening hospital stay: 12 healthy volunteers with prior experience of MDA, or of both MDMA and a classical psychedelic, received oral racemic MDA 1.4 mg/kg (absolute doses 83–128 mg) and an identical lactose placebo capsule on consecutive days, half of them in each order (how the order was assigned is not stated). MDA results were compared with MDMA data (1.5 mg/kg oral racemic MDMA and its placebo) from two separate, earlier placebo-controlled studies by the same group (Baggott et al., 2016a, 2016b): this MDA-versus-MDMA comparison is between different people and was not randomized. Measures: the 66-item Altered States of Consciousness rating scale (peak ratings given at 8 h), visual analogue scales repeatedly up to 8 h (6 h in the MDMA data), the Affect Valuation Index and Interpersonal Adjective Scales-Revised before and 2.5 h after dosing, heart rate and blood pressure hourly, prolactin and cortisol at 2 and 3 h, and plasma MDA and its metabolite HMA up to 30 h. Mixed-effects models (condition fixed, participant random) with Westfall-corrected pairwise comparisons; visual and global psychedelic measures from this trial were published earlier (Baggott et al., 2010).
can_establish: That in 12 healthy volunteers with prior psychedelic or MDA experience, MDA at the study's single dose raised self-rated drug effects, closeness to others, perceptual and other psychedelic-type effects, heart rate, blood pressure, prolactin and cortisol compared with placebo taken by the same people, and how MDA and its metabolite HMA rose and fell in blood over 30 hours.
cannot_establish: How MDA and MDMA differ within the same people: the MDMA data come from other participants in separate studies, not randomized against MDA, with visual analogue and heart-rate data recorded to 6 h against 8 h for MDA, so differences in duration, kind of effect or heart-rate rise may reflect who was studied and how long they were observed rather than the drugs; nor anything about other doses, repeated use, settings outside a hospital, women in particular, or uncommon harms (12 people, no adverse-event data).

sample.recruitment: Not described in the paper (the acknowledgments thank staff for help with participant recruitment); payment not stated. Eligibility required self-reported prior experience with MDA alone, or with both MDMA and a classical serotonergic psychedelic such as LSD (PDF p. 3, printed p. 2, Material and methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy; prior MDA experience, or MDMA plus a classical psychedelic; no DSM-IV drug dependence other than nicotine or caffeine. Screening by history and physical examination, self-reported drug history, 12-lead ECG, liver panel and blood chemistry; pregnancy and drug toxicology tests before drug administration; effective contraception requested. Nicotine was forbidden during the hospital stay and caffeine from 10 h before dosing (PDF p. 3, printed p. 2).
sample.demographics: Age 27.8 (SD 8) years; 14.8 (SD 2) years of education; two Hispanic or Latino (one Caucasian, one of African American ancestry) and ten not Hispanic or Latino (Caucasian); weight 74.1 (SD 9.2) kg (PDF p. 4, printed p. 3, Results › Participants). The number of women is not given; the limitations mention a low number of female participants (PDF p. 9, printed p. 8).
sample.attrition: All 12 enrolled participants completed the study (PDF p. 4, printed p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: A small group of screened healthy volunteers with prior psychedelic or MDA experience, without drug dependence and with few women. They may expect, recognise and tolerate the effects differently from people taking MDA for the first time, and people with heart disease were excluded (the authors note that the blood-pressure rises could concern people with cardiovascular disease, PDF p. 9, printed p. 8). The MDMA comparison participants were recruited for other studies; their characteristics are not reported in this paper.

exposure.measurement: Given in the laboratory: racemic MDA synthesized by the researchers, with identity and purity confirmed by melting point, proton nuclear magnetic resonance (300 MHz) and elemental analysis under an FDA Investigational New Drug exemption; placebo was lactose in an identical gelatin capsule (PDF p. 3, printed p. 2, Drugs and dosing).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one oral dose of racemic MDA 1.4 mg/kg body weight (absolute doses 83–128 mg) after a two-hour fast, and placebo, on consecutive days (PDF pp. 3–4, printed pp. 2–3). The MDMA comparison studies gave single oral doses of racemic MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, which the authors describe as isomolar to the MDA dose (PDF p. 3, printed p. 2). One dose level of each drug.
exposure.polysubstance: Drug dependence other than nicotine or caffeine excluded; drug toxicology tests before dosing (results not reported); nicotine and caffeine restricted during the stay. Past use of other drugs beyond the experience required for eligibility is not quantified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Drug toxicology and pregnancy tests before drug administration; nicotine forbidden during the stay and caffeine from 10 h before dosing (PDF p. 3, printed p. 2). MDA and its metabolite were still detectable on the day after MDA, when half the participants had their placebo session (PDF p. 4, printed p. 3).

comparison.controls: Within-person lactose placebo in the same 12 people, on the day before or after MDA. For drug comparisons, MDMA (1.5 mg/kg) and placebo data from two earlier placebo-controlled studies by the same group (Baggott et al., 2016a, 2016b); MDA was compared only with its own placebo, and MDMA only with the placebo of the MDMA studies (PDF pp. 3–4, printed pp. 2–3).
comparison.matching: None between the MDA and MDMA samples: they are different people, their number varies by measure (N = 12 in Figures 1 and 3; N = 16 in Figure 2 and Table 1), and the MDMA participants' characteristics are not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No comparison of the MDA and MDMA samples on age, sex, prior drug experience or expectations is reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for the MDMA comparison participants.

outcomes.instruments: Altered States of Consciousness rating scale (66 items; the three original main scales and 11 lower-order factors; translated into English for the study by a professional translator and back-translated; given 8 h after dosing for retrospective peak ratings); visual analogue scales for general drug effects, stimulant or MDMA-like effects and psychedelic-like effects, repeatedly up to 8 h (questions on time distortion and closed-eye imagery asked after a timed 30 s with eyes closed); Affect Valuation Index and Interpersonal Adjective Scales-Revised before and 2.5 h after dosing; heart rate and blood pressure before and hourly to 8 h (6 h in the MDMA data); serum prolactin and cortisol before and 2 and 3 h after dosing; plasma MDA and HMA by two-dimensional GC/MS before and 1–30 h after dosing (PDF pp. 3–4, printed pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: The altered-states scale is validated in German; the English version was not separately validated. Visual analogue items are ad hoc. Computerized tasks are listed among the timed measures but no results are reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Baseline-corrected maximum effect (Emax) or area under the effect-time curve (AUC); longer duration tested as baseline-corrected scores at 6 h and 8 h for the five general drug-effect items.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Westfall correction for pairwise comparisons after a significant effect of condition; no correction across the 46 or more outcomes (14 altered-states scales, 23 visual analogue items, four affect and social dimensions, three cardiovascular and two hormone measures), several analysed as both Emax and AUC.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind for MDA against placebo; no blinding is possible across studies, since the MDMA data were collected separately. Whether participants could tell MDA from placebo was not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals. Visual analogue areas (Table 1, mean ± SEM; MDA, MDMA, placebo for MDA, placebo for MDMA): any drug effect 402.5 ± 46, 270.3 ± 21, 4.7 ± 3, 17.8 ± 11; good drug effect 461.1 ± 43, 276.9 ± 20; drug liking 502.5 ± 50, 269.1 ± 29; stimulated 350.4 ± 53, 222.5 ± 20; closeness to others 168.0 ± 53, 114.4 ± 44 (MDA vs MDMA not significant); time distortions 321.6 ± 46, 143.0 ± 31; patterns seen with closed eyes 174.3 ± 58, 70.1 ± 24; bad drug effect 47.9 ± 26, 41.4 ± 16 (neither differed from placebo). At 6 h any drug effect was 41.6 ± 7 higher after MDA than MDMA (z = 6.3) and 46.4 ± 7 above placebo (z = 6.7); at 8 h 35.6 ± 10 above placebo (t = 3.7, p = 0.001). Altered-states scales (Figure 1), F(3,21) from 5.09 to 35.9. Affect: arousal F(3,68) = 5.30, p = 0.002; valence F(3,68) = 2.35, p = 0.08. Heart rate rise 20 ± 3 bpm (MDA) vs 30.6 ± 4.5 (MDMA), p = 0.03; systolic 33 ± 2 vs 31 ± 3 mmHg; diastolic 24 ± 2 vs 19 ± 2 mmHg, p = 0.06. Prolactin rise 16 ± 6 vs 29 ± 6 ng/mL (p = 0.07); cortisol 16 ± 1 vs 13 ± 2 µg/dL. MDA pharmacokinetics (mean ± SD): peak 229 ± 39 µg/L, AUC0–∞ 3,636 ± 958 h·µg/L, half-life 10.9 ± 4 h.
analysis.covariates: None; drug condition as fixed effect and participant as random effect.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration is reported in the paper. The earlier report of this trial's visual measures (Baggott et al., 2010) was not among the files read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Measures from this trial on visual changes were reported elsewhere; computerized tasks listed among the measures are not reported; peak (Emax) comparisons of the visual analogue items are 'not shown'; no adverse events are reported although the abstract says MDA was well tolerated; affect and social results are shown in a figure without statistics for Affiliation.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors note that comparing with MDMA data from separate studies reduced power (PDF p. 9, printed p. 8).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 12 experienced volunteers, MDA raised self-rated drug effects, closeness to others, perceptual changes, heart rate, blood pressure, prolactin and cortisol compared with placebo. Against MDMA data from other people in earlier studies, MDA's self-rated effects were still raised at 6–8 h when MDMA's were no longer raised at 6 h (MDMA was not recorded beyond 6 h), MDA was rated higher on closed-eye imagery and spiritual experience and lower on anxiety, dread of ego dissolution and impaired control, and MDA raised heart rate less (20 vs 30.6 bpm).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says MDA raised heart rate, blood pressure, cortisol and prolactin to a degree similar to MDMA (PDF p. 2, printed p. 1) and the discussion that the heart-rate and blood-pressure rises were similar to MDMA's (PDF p. 9, printed p. 8), whereas the heart-rate rise after MDA was significantly smaller (p = 0.03) and the prolactin rise about half, as a trend (p = 0.07) (PDF p. 5, printed p. 4). The abstract states that MDA was well tolerated without any adverse-event data in the paper. It concludes that similar pharmacokinetics point to pharmacodynamics, not kinetics, as the reason for MDA's longer effects, while the discussion says the difference may be due to MDA's longer half-life (PDF p. 9, printed p. 8); the MDMA kinetics compared come from another group's study (Kolbrich et al., 2008a, 1.6 mg/kg), not from this one. A more introverted, emotionally intense state after MDA against a more extraverted one after MDMA is offered as a qualitative impression with no data (PDF p. 8, printed p. 7). Above all, every MDA–MDMA difference comes from a non-randomized comparison across separate studies with unequal recording times, which the abstract presents simply as a comparison with the authors' prior similar studies.

timeline.event: Baggott et al. (2010), PLoS One: visual changes and global psychedelic effects from this same MDA trial, described in its title as a randomized controlled trial (named in the methods of this paper; not read here)
Baggott et al. (2016a; 2016b): the two placebo-controlled MDMA studies (1.5 mg/kg) whose data supply the MDMA comparison in this paper (not read here)
This paper: presented by the authors as the first controlled study of MDA in humans in over 35 years and the first measurement of its pharmacokinetics in humans

replication.where_it_stands: The authors cite no earlier modern controlled human study of MDA; older controlled studies (Turek et al., 1974; Yensen et al., 1976) predate the spread of MDMA (introduction, PDF p. 2). No within-person randomized comparison of MDA with MDMA is reported.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse [DA017716, DA016776] and the NIH National Center for Research Resources [UCSF-CTSI UL1 RR024131] (PDF p. 10, printed p. 9, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (PDF p. 10, printed p. 9, Disclosure statement).
funding.affiliations_note: Friends Research Institute (San Francisco), the NIDA Intramural Research Program and Thomas Jefferson University; the first author's present address is a pharmaceutical company (Genentech Inc.) (PDF p. 2, printed p. 1). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, double-blind crossover study giving MDA, MDMA and placebo to the same people, with the same recording window for both drugs (at least 12 h), more than one dose, sessions spaced well apart rather than on consecutive days, equal numbers of women and men, and systematic recording of adverse events.

domains.note: Half the participants had placebo after MDA and half before; how the order was assigned (random or not) is not stated.

MDA and placebo on consecutive days, with MDA and its metabolite still detectable on the second day (PDF p. 4). Placebo-only models found no significant sequence effect, but with six people per sequence; the authors concede residual effects may have lowered sensitivity (PDF p. 9).
Identical capsules, but experienced volunteers are likely to recognise MDA; no check of the blind.
All 12 completed. The MDMA comparison N varies between analyses without explanation (see the editors' domain below).
Self-ratings by participants who probably knew the condition; the English altered-states scale is unvalidated; heart rate, blood pressure, hormones and drug levels are objective.

No registration reported; many outcomes without correction across them; peak comparisons 'not shown'; computerized tasks and adverse events not reported; figure references in the text do not match the figures.

domains.domain: Comparison of MDA with MDMA (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Different people from separate earlier studies, not randomized, with unequal recording windows (8 h vs 6 h), unequal and unexplained N, and no description of the MDMA participants.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: MDA against placebo in the same 12 people is a placebo-controlled comparison with large effects on self-ratings and on heart rate and blood pressure, but consecutive-day dosing with MDA still in the blood the next day, no reported registration and unreported outcomes lower confidence. The MDA-versus-MDMA comparison, which is what the paper is mostly used for, is a non-randomized comparison across studies with unequal recording windows. The paper may be cited for MDA's effects compared with placebo in experienced healthy volunteers at one dose, for MDA's pharmacokinetics in 12 people, and, as a weak cross-study comparison, for the pattern that MDA's self-rated effects lasted longer and included more closed-eye imagery and less anxiety than MDMA's in other people. It may not be cited for a firm difference between the two drugs in duration, heart-rate rise or kind of effect, for safety (no adverse-event data), or for any comparison of strength.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 12 healthy volunteers with prior experience of MDA, or of both MDMA and a classical psychedelic, and no drug dependence other than nicotine or caffeine, received one oral dose of racemic MDA 1.4 mg/kg (absolute doses 83–128 mg) and an identical placebo on consecutive days during one hospital stay, double-blind; half had placebo on the day after MDA. All 12 completed; mean age 27.8 (SD 8) years; the number of women is not reported.
key_findings.locator: Material and methods › Participants; Drugs and dosing (printed p. 2); Results › Participants; Checking for sequence effects (printed p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The MDMA comparison data come from two separate earlier placebo-controlled studies by the same group (1.5 mg/kg oral racemic MDMA); MDA was compared only with its own placebo and MDMA only with the MDMA studies' placebo. Heart rate and blood pressure were recorded hourly to 8 h after MDA but to 6 h in the MDMA data, and the MDMA data have N = 16 for the visual analogue scales and N = 12 for the altered-states and affect and social scales.
key_findings.locator: Material and methods › Source of MDMA comparison data (printed p. 2); Physiological, endocrine, and pharmacokinetic effects; Statistical analysis (printed p. 3); legends of Figures 1–3 and Table 1 (printed pp. 4–7)

key_findings.finding: Over the whole session (area under the curve, mean ± SEM), MDA scored higher than MDMA on any drug effect (402.5 ± 46 vs 270.3 ± 21), good drug effect (461.1 ± 43 vs 276.9 ± 20), high (416.9 ± 52 vs 263.4 ± 25), drug liking (502.5 ± 50 vs 269.1 ± 29), stimulated (350.4 ± 53 vs 222.5 ± 20), time distortions (321.6 ± 46 vs 143.0 ± 31) and patterns seen with closed eyes (174.3 ± 58 vs 70.1 ± 24); on peak effects the two drugs largely did not differ (data not shown).
key_findings.note: The MDMA visual analogue data run to 6 h only, against 8 h for MDA (Figure 2, PDF p. 6), and the paper does not say whether the areas were computed over the same window; part of MDA's larger areas may come from the longer recording. Table 1's statistics column is headed Emax although its values are areas (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Finding text confirmed; note corrected to: No MDMA values are shown at 8 h (Figure 2; the methods state a 6-h limit for MDMA only for heart rate and blood pressure), so the 8-h result compares MDA with placebo only.
key_findings.note: MDMA was not recorded at 8 h, so the 8-h result compares MDA with placebo only.

key_findings.finding: MDA raised self-rated closeness to others compared with its placebo (area 168.0 ± 53 vs 11.5 ± 38), not significantly different from MDMA (114.4 ± 44); insightful (143.2 ± 36) and new meanings (235.8 ± 69) were also raised by MDA and did not differ from MDMA. On the interpersonal adjective scale only MDMA increased Affiliation (no statistic printed); arousal on the affect index changed with condition (F(3,68) = 5.30, p = 0.002) similarly for both drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Affect and social functioning (printed pp. 3–4); Table 1 (printed p. 6)

key_findings.finding: On the Altered States of Consciousness scale (peak ratings given at 8 h; F(3,21) printed for each scale), MDA was rated higher than MDMA on complex imagery (F = 20.6), elementary imagery (F = 13.9) and spiritual experience (F = 24.8), and MDMA higher than MDA on dread of ego dissolution (F = 15.1), impaired control and cognition (F = 11.1) and anxiety (F = 5.09, p = 0.008); on these last three MDA did not differ from placebo. Audio-visual synesthesia was raised by MDA only (F = 8.26). Both drugs raised oceanic boundlessness, visionary changes, blissful state, insightfulness, changed meaning of percepts, experience of unity and disembodiment.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (printed p. 4): F values and pairwise results printed beside each scale
key_findings.note: The F values and pairwise results are printed inside the Figure 1 image, not in the PDF's text layer, so a mechanical text check will not find them; they were read on a 300-dpi rendering. Means are only plotted; their values were not extracted. N = 12 for both drugs in this figure.

key_findings.finding: On the visual analogue scales, bad drug effect (area 47.9 ± 26 after MDA, 41.4 ± 16 after MDMA) did not differ significantly from placebo for either drug (effect of condition F(3,21) = 3.1, p = 0.0487, all pairwise comparisons not significant); anxious, relaxed, clear-headed, objects or beings seen with closed eyes and paranoia showed no significant effect of condition. No adverse-event data are reported in the paper. [Relaxed, clear-headed and closed-eye objects or beings are not unwanted effects, so the 'Unwanted effects' heading is dropped.]

Heart rate rose by 20 ± 3 bpm after MDA, significantly less than the 30.6 ± 4.5 bpm rise after MDMA (p = 0.03); peak systolic blood pressure rose by 33 ± 2 mmHg after MDA and 31 ± 3 after MDMA, and diastolic by 24 ± 2 and 19 ± 2 mmHg (a non-significant trend, p = 0.06). Effects of condition: heart rate F(3,22) = 17.1, diastolic F(3,22) = 32.4, systolic F(3,22) = 61.7, all p < 0.0001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Physiological and endocrine measures › Physiological changes (printed p. 4)
key_findings.note: The ± is not defined in this paragraph (Table 1 uses SEM). MDA was recorded to 8 h and MDMA to 6 h, in different people.

key_findings.finding: Prolactin rose by 16 ± 6 ng/mL after MDA and 29 ± 6 ng/mL after MDMA compared with placebo (F(3,25) = 13.0, p < 0.0001; MDMA higher as a non-significant trend, p = 0.07); cortisol rose by 16 ± 1 µg/dL after MDA and 13 ± 2 µg/dL after MDMA (F(3,24) = 43.1, p < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Physiological and endocrine measures › Endocrine changes (printed p. 4)

key_findings.finding: MDA pharmacokinetics (mean ± SD; the number analysed is not stated, 12 took part): peak plasma concentration 229 ± 39 µg/L, AUC0–∞ 3,636 ± 958 h·µg/L, elimination half-life 10.9 ± 4 h, clearance/F 30,267 ± 8,214 mL/min. The metabolite HMA peaked at 92 ± 61 µg/L (AUC 1,544 ± 741; half-life 14.1 ± 3 h in the results, 14.1 ± 3.5 h in the discussion), and its peak and AUC varied over seven-fold and four-fold between people.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics (printed p. 5); AUC units from Discussion, 6th paragraph (printed p. 8, right column)

key_findings.finding: MDA and its metabolite were still detectable on the day after dosing, so half the placebo sessions took place with residual MDA in the blood; models of placebo sessions only (placebo after MDA, placebo before MDA, and the MDMA studies' placebo) found no significant sequence effects on physiological, endocrine and visual analogue measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Checking for sequence effects (printed p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret MDA as having significant entactogen, stimulant and psychedelic effects, and MDMA strong entactogen, modest stimulant and weak psychedelic effects; qualitatively, they say MDA appeared to produce a more introverted, emotionally intense prosocial state and MDMA seemed to encourage a more extraverted, gregarious one, an impression for which they cite no statistic (Figure 3 plots the Gregarious and Aloof octants without tests).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (printed p. 7, right column) and 4th paragraph (printed p. 8, left column)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: MDA and placebo on consecutive days, which may have let residual MDA alter half the placebo sessions; comparison with MDMA data from separate studies, which reduced power; racemic forms only; and a modest sample, few women and single dose levels, which they say prevent full characterization of MDA's pharmacokinetics.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure references are swapped: the text cites Figure 2 for the affect and social (AVI and IASR) results and Figure 3 for the visual analogue scales, but Figure 2 shows the visual analogue time courses and Figure 3 the affect and social circumplex.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers following the text look in the wrong figure; no value changes.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's statistics column is headed 'Effect of Condition on Emax' while its values are areas under the curve, and the text says peak (Emax) differences between the drugs were not shown and largely absent; whether the F tests and the >, < and ≈ symbols refer to areas or to peaks is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The significance of the reported MDA–MDMA differences in areas is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Heart rate and blood pressure were recorded to 6 h for MDMA against 8 h for MDA (Methods), Figure 2 shows no MDMA visual analogue values after 6 h, and the window used for the areas is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: MDA's larger areas cannot be separated from the unequal observation time; the duration difference rests on the 6-h comparison, since no MDMA data are reported at 8 h. (The abstract's 'resolved by 6 h' is itself supported by the 6-h data.)

reporting_issues.issue: The number of MDMA participants differs between analyses (N = 12 in Figures 1 and 3; N = 16 in Figure 2 and Table 1) without explanation, and denominator degrees of freedom vary from 21 to 68 across analyses with 12 MDA participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: Who contributed to each comparison cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The valence dimension of the affect index is described as showing a significant effect of condition at F(3,68) = 2.35, p = 0.08, above the paper's stated 0.05 level.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only arousal changed significantly; valence did not.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of women and the method of assigning session order are not reported (half had placebo after MDA; the limitations mention a low number of female participants).
reporting_issues.consequence: Applicability to women cannot be judged, and the order allocation cannot be appraised.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says MDA was well tolerated and the methods describe extensive safety monitoring and a two-week follow-up visit, but no adverse events or follow-up findings are reported; computerized tasks listed among the measures are not reported either.
reporting_issues.consequence: Tolerability cannot be checked from the paper, and some collected outcomes are unreported.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the AUC0–∞ of MDA and HMA in µg/L; the discussion gives h·µg/L.
reporting_issues.consequence: A unit error in the abstract; the values are unchanged.
